title: Generations, Small Object Heap, and Large Object Heap (SOH and LOH)
hook: The garbage collector divides the managed heap into generations so short-lived objects die fast. The Small Object Heap (SOH) holds most objects; the Large Object Heap (LOH) holds allocations roughly 85,000 bytes and larger.

blocks.text: Generation 0 is a nursery for brand-new allocations. Objects that survive a collection are promoted to generation 1, then generation 2. The SOH is collected frequently and compacted. The LOH stores large arrays and strings at or above roughly 85,000 bytes; it is collected with generation 2. Since .NET 4.5.1 LOH can be compacted on demand; .NET 5+ added the Pinned Object Heap (POH) so short-lived pinned buffers no longer fragment the SOH.

entries.plainDefinition: Heap region for objects under the large-object threshold.
entries.example: A List<int> with ten items lives on the SOH.

entries.plainDefinition: Heap region for allocations at or above ~85,000 bytes.
entries.example: A 90 KB byte[] for a CSV row buffer lands on the LOH.

entries.plainDefinition: Moving a surviving object to an older generation.
entries.example: A singleton cache entry promoted to gen 2 stays until a full collection.

entries.plainDefinition: Dedicated heap segment for pinned objects so they do not block SOH compaction.
entries.example: A GCHandle.Alloc with Pinned type places the object on the POH in .NET 5+.

blocks.text: Most allocations die young. Nursery collections are cheap. A service that allocates one giant buffer per request pays generation-2 and LOH costs instead of quick gen-0 reclaims. Understanding SOH versus LOH explains why pooling and streaming matter for CSV imports and image buffers.

blocks.title: LOH threshold rule of thumb
blocks.body: Arrays and strings at or above ~85,000 bytes go to the LOH. Prefer ArrayPool<byte>, chunking, or streaming when you do not need one contiguous giant buffer.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Allocate in gen 0
items.body: new bumps a pointer in the nursery — very fast.

items.title: Survive a collection
items.body: Live objects are marked and promoted to gen 1.

items.title: Survive again
items.body: Promoted to gen 2 — collected less often, more expensive.

items.title: Large allocation
items.body: Size at threshold skips nursery semantics and lands on LOH.

items.title: Pinned allocation
items.body: Pinned objects go to POH (.NET 5+) instead of blocking SOH compaction.

diagram.title: Generations and heaps

flowchart TD

  B -->|survives| C[Gen 1 SOH]
  C -->|survives| D[Gen 2 SOH]
  E[large array 85KB+] --> F[LOH]

snippet.label: Small vs large allocation
snippet.code:
var small = new byte[1024];       // SOH, gen 0
var large = new byte[90_000];     // LOH
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(small)); // often 0
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(large)); // 2 for LOH objects
snippet.explanation: Size determines heap segment. LOH objects start in generation 2.

snippet.label: ArrayPool instead of LOH churn
snippet.explanation: Renting reuses arrays instead of allocating a new LOH object every request.

snippet.label: Check LOH compaction mode
snippet.explanation: Modern .NET can compact LOH on demand or when a heap hard limit is hit.

snippet.label: Trigger LOH compaction once
snippet.explanation: CompactOnce defragments LOH on the next full GC. Use after a burst of large transient buffers, not in request handlers.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming every new byte[] is gen 0 — large arrays skip to LOH. Holding references to gen-2 caches that pin old graphs alive. Ignoring LOH fragmentation in long-running imports.

blocks.text: The LOH threshold is roughly 85,000 bytes for single-dimensional arrays. LOH objects start in generation 2 and are not compacted by default — free-list fragmentation is the production risk. Since .NET 4.5.1 you can set GCLargeObjectHeapCompactionMode.CompactOnce; container heap hard limits can trigger compaction automatically. .NET 5 introduced the Pinned Object Heap (POH) so interop pinning no longer creates immovable holes in the SOH. How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters shows gc-heap-size and loh-size; a gen-2 spike after CSV imports with flat live object count signals LOH fragmentation.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming LOH is never compacted (wrong since .NET 4.5.1) or that every byte[] is gen 0. Strong answer: size threshold, gen-2 collection, optional compaction, POH for pins, ArrayPool for reuse.

interviewTakeaways: Gen 0 is a nursery; promotion means the object survived a collection and moved to an older generation.
LOH is ~85 KB+; collected with gen 2; fragmentation is the risk unless you compact or pool.
For CSV imports and image buffers, rent from ArrayPool or stream chunks instead of per-request LOH allocations.
60s: SOH has gens 0–2 and compacts. LOH is 85 KB+, gen 2 only, fragments unless CompactOnce. POH holds pins since .NET 5. Pool large buffers.
Follow-up: what triggers LOH compaction in a container with GCHeapHardLimitPercent?
commonPitfalls: Treating a 100 KB buffer like a cheap gen-0 allocation — that answer ignores the LOH threshold.
Strong answer: name the ~85 KB threshold, gen-2 collection cost, and ArrayPool or streaming alternative.
Never returning rented arrays to ArrayPool.
Assuming LOH is never compacted — CompactOnce and heap hard limits can defragment.

jsTsCorrelations.note: V8 is generational too, but you do not tune an LOH threshold the same way. Large TypedArrays still live in the JS heap.
Node Buffer.alloc creates heap objects with no separate LOH segment. In C# a 90 KB byte[] has explicit LOH semantics and gen-2 collection behavior you can reason about.
